text:
Chris Ballard’s September 2012 Sports Illustrated cover story (titled “The Full Gronkowski” on the magazine and also known as “The Last Happy Man”) is a personality profile of then-23-year-old Patriots tight end Rob Gronkowski at the peak of his early fame.

The piece contrasts Gronk’s on-field dominance—he had just set NFL tight-end records with 1,327 receiving yards and 17 touchdowns in 2011—with his off-field life as an unfiltered, joyful party animal. Ballard spent time with him, including at a 21st-birthday party in Massachusetts for which Gronkowski was paid five figures to appear. There, hungover from the night before, Gronk still took charge: he organized a shotgun-beer contest (puncturing cans with his thumb like a pro), then played beer pong and flip cup without acting like a celebrity. He high-fived after misses, laughed off losses, and treated everyone the same.

Gronkowski explained his lifestyle to Ballard: he worked out two hours a day and then had 12 hours free. With no girlfriend or kids, sitting at home felt unproductive and boring, so he said yes to parties, charity events, and paid appearances. His father noted he was being offered “stupid money” he couldn’t turn down. Ballard portrayed him not as a reckless frat boy but as a genuine, gracious 23-year-old who simply loved having fun and meeting people—the “last happy man” in a league full of calculated images.

The article also touched on his close-knit family of athletic brothers, his work ethic, and how his larger-than-life personality made him both a marketing magnet and a unique force on the field. It captured Gronk at the start of his “Summer of Gronk” era, when his combination of production and personality made him one of the NFL’s most magnetic stars.

text:
Ontario trains nurses, then watches them drive across the border to work.

Our new report found an estimated 2,218 nurses lived in Ontario but commuted to Michigan for work in 2025, up from 1,887 in 2023. We surveyed more than 200 nurses in Windsor to find out why.

The top reason was not what many people assume. It was the availability of work with a schedule they wanted, at 44%, ahead of compensation at 29%. As of August 13, just one of 16 was full-time nursing jobs posted on Windsor hospitals' websites was part-time or casual. New graduates want full-time work, and Ontario keeps offering the opposite.

The findings go further. 68% said health care technology and equipment is worse in Canada, with only 2% saying it is better. 62% said working in a government-run facility was not important to them.

These nurses are not lost to the profession. They are working full shifts a few kilometres away. If Ontario followed the Swedish model and let non-profit and for-profit hospitals into the market, those employers could offer nurses what they are asking for.

This erupted into a brawl where Vinnie bashed Les and Reg Mikkelsen bashed and threated Brian with a knife as kids. The Mikkelsen father had died so Reg the eldest son would scavenge chicken necks and potato skins from bins for them to eat. As adults Brian Kane was easily the most feared man in Melbourne, closely followed by his schizo brother Les. Even podcasts now with old prison guards say Brian was the most dangerous with his fists. The two crews were at war over the fallout of the robbery and basically a long history of hatred. text:
LSU Just Won a Major Legal Battle. The Bigger Fight Starts Now.

LSU and the players challenging the NCAA and SEC just won an important victory in Louisiana court, but this is not the final word. Judge William Jorden granted preliminary injunctive relief protecting the affected athletes seeking another season of college eligibility, and just as importantly, the ruling protects LSU from NCAA and SEC punishment for using those players while the case continues. The court did not rule that former professional players now have a permanent right to return to college football. It ruled that these particular athletes have shown enough legal merit, and enough potential for irreparable harm, that they should not lose an entire season while the lawsuit is being decided.

In plain English, the players have won the right to keep playing while the court decides who ultimately wins the case. This case is much narrower than the headlines make it sound. The legal question is not simply whether former NFL players should be allowed back into college football. The stronger question is whether an athlete can be told his college eligibility is finished, make an irreversible career decision based on that rule, and then be denied the benefit of a new eligibility rule because of the decision the old rule caused him to make.

That is where the NCAA and SEC have a real problem. These players were operating under a system that told them their college careers were over, so some of them moved into the NFL process because there appeared to be no college option left. Then the eligibility structure changed. Now the NCAA and SEC want to use those professional decisions against the same athletes who made them under the old rules. That creates a legitimate fairness and reliance issue, and it gives the players a much stronger argument than simply saying they should be able to move freely between college and professional football.

Dae'Quan Wright testified that he would not have pursued the NFL had he known another college season might become available. Zxavian Harris offered similar testimony. Wright received a $25,000 signing bonus and even offered to repay it. Players are not arguing for an open door between college and the NFL. They are arguing that the rules changed after they had already acted on the rules they were given.

The money issue also exposes how much college football has changed. For decades, the distinction between college athletes and professional athletes was easy to explain because professionals were paid and college athletes were not. That line no longer exists in any meaningful way. College athletes can now earn enormous amounts through NIL arrangements and revenue sharing, and in some cases they may earn more than players who briefly spend time in professional football.

That does not make college football and the NFL legally identical. Professional contracts, draft participation, roster status, employment relationships, and league structure still matter. What has disappeared is the old argument that receiving money automatically creates a clear moral or legal dividing line. If one athlete can earn seven figures in college while another receives a relatively modest professional signing bonus, then compensation by itself is no longer enough to explain why one remains eligible and the other becomes permanently disqualified.

The SEC did have a respectable argument available. LSU voluntarily belongs to the conference, membership comes with rules, and the conference has a legitimate interest in competitive balance and eligibility standards. The trouble came when the SEC built a punishment structure strong enough that LSU could have been forced to bench players even if a court had already protected those players from NCAA enforcement.

That creates an obvious legal problem. If a court says the NCAA cannot stop a player from participating, the SEC cannot necessarily accomplish the same result indirectly by threatening LSU with such severe punishment that the school has no realistic choice but to sit him. At some point, indirect punishment becomes functionally identical to direct prohibition. Judge Jorden appears to have recognized that, which is why the protection given to LSU may be just as important as the protection given to the players.

The next phase is even more interesting because the SEC has opened a second front in federal court. While the Louisiana case was unfolding, the conference filed a separate lawsuit against LSU in Alabama and changed the nature of the legal fight. Instead of relying only on eligibility rules, the SEC is now making a First Amendment argument based on expressive association.

The SEC is essentially saying that it has a constitutional right to determine the standards under which its members associate and that LSU, as a public institution, cannot force the conference to accept conduct that conflicts with its rules and stated mission. That is a more sophisticated argument than simply declaring the players ineligible, and it deserves to be taken seriously. It is also nowhere near a guaranteed winner.

The central question may become who is actually forcing the SEC to associate. LSU is not simply ordering the conference to abandon its rules. A Louisiana court is restricting how those rules may be enforced against certain players and against LSU. That difference could become critical because the federal case may raise questions involving jurisdiction, state authority, federal constitutional law, sovereign immunity, parallel litigation, and the relationship between a public university and a private athletic conference.

This fight is also worth taking seriously because Judge Jorden did not give LSU and the players everything they wanted. He ruled against portions of their case and found that many plaintiffs did not have sufficient connection to the SEC to pursue certain claims against the conference. That tells me he was separating the legal issues rather than simply handing the home side a victory. He ruled for the SEC where he believed the law required it, then granted substantial protection where he believed the players had made the stronger case.

For LSU, the immediate effect is significant. The school can presently place the protected players on its roster without facing the NCAA and SEC penalties that had been hanging over the program. That does not mean every player can walk straight onto the field because other practice and game eligibility requirements may still apply, but the biggest legal obstacle has been removed for now.

The next major development will likely come from the federal court in Alabama. The SEC can seek emergency relief there, the NCAA and SEC can pursue appellate review of the Louisiana injunction, and LSU will almost certainly preserve the players' roster status while the current order remains in effect. The most dangerous scenario for LSU would be a federal order that directly conflicts with the Louisiana ruling because that would turn an eligibility dispute into a much more complicated fight over federal and state judicial authority.

At this point, I still give the legal advantage to LSU and the players, roughly 70 percent to 30 percent. That is not because I believe former professional athletes should automatically be allowed to return to college sports. Conferences have a legitimate interest in drawing a line between college and professional competition. The weakness in the NCAA and SEC position is how these particular athletes crossed that line.

They were told their college eligibility was finished, they acted on that information, and then the rules changed. Now the same organizations that changed the rules want to use the players' earlier decisions as the reason they cannot benefit from the new system. That is where the equities turn against the governing bodies.

Tonight was a major legal victory for LSU and the players, but the larger story is only beginning. The SEC has moved the battle into federal court and transformed what began as an eligibility dispute into a much broader question about the power of athletic conferences, the rights of member universities, and the limits of conference enforcement when a court order points the other way. The next ruling may decide much more than whether a few football players receive another season. It could help define how much independent power conferences like the SEC actually have when their rules collide with a court protecting one of their own member schools.

text:
Yoruba people, don't keep quiet again.

If you like, call me a “bigot”. Name calling is the littlest of price i have to pay but i need to set some records straight.

Not because we hate anybody. Not because we are competing with anybody.

But because we have realised that if we don't document our history, teach our children and correct false narratives, the next generation may grow up knowing a distorted version of their own history.

Look around.

1. Wole Soyinka :  Nobel Prize.
Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986. 

Yet we now see people spreading the story that Achebe was offered the Nobel and rejected it. 

Where is the evidence? The Nobel committee keeps nomination records secret for 50 years.

2. Fela Kuti: Afrobeat.

Fela is widely recognised as the pioneer/father of Afrobeat. Give credit to everyone who contributed, but don't rewrite who pioneered the genre.

3. Hubert Ogunde : Theatre.

Ogunde was a pioneer of modern Nigerian theatre and founded the first contemporary professional theatrical company in Nigeria.

4. Samuel Ajayi Crowther:  Church history.

A Yoruba-born man who became the first African Anglican bishop. 

This is African history that deserves to be properly taught.

5. Sir Adetokunbo Ademola.

He was the first Nigerian to serve as Chief Justice of Nigeria. 

That is a major part of Nigeria's judicial history.

6. Duro Ladipo and Yoruba theatre.

He took Yoruba mythology, history, music and folklore to the stage in a way that gained international attention.

His Oba Koso became internationally acclaimed.

7. Adire : Fashion.

Adire is not just “African print.” It is a historic Yoruba textile tradition, traditionally produced by Yoruba women in southwestern Nigeria.

8. Aso-Oke : Fashion.

Aso-Oke/Aso-Ofi is a historic Yoruba handwoven textile tradition. 

Iseyin and other Yoruba communities have carried this craft for generations.

9. Aso-Ebi : Social culture.

Even the idea and name of Aso-Ebi come from Yoruba culture, clothing used to identify family, friends and groups during important ceremonies.

10. Amala : Food.

Amala is deeply rooted in Yoruba food culture and became one of the foods most strongly associated with Yorubaland.

11. Ofada Rice : Food.

The name itself comes from Ofada in Ogun State. 

Yet how many young Nigerians actually know the history behind the name?

12. Yoruba textiles and dressing generally.

Aso-Oke and Adire are not simply clothes. 

They carry identity, status, history and culture.

So yes, Yoruba people must open their eyes.

We must research.

We must write books.

We must preserve archives.

We must make documentaries.

We must teach our children.

We must correct false claims with evidence.

And let me make this clear:

We don't need to steal anybody's history to celebrate Yoruba history.

Give everyone their credit.

But give Yoruba people their credit too.

The generation coming behind us deserves to know who did what, where it started and how it developed.

If we remain silent, repetition will eventually become “history.”

This is the time to document our history.

This is the time to defend our history.

This is the time to teach our children.

Not with hate.

With facts.

End

text:
Von Miller wanted his number 40 back when he joined the Cowboys. But there was one problem, it belonged to his teammate Hunter Luepke. And the only way to get it was to give up equity from a chicken business. Miller first offered a lifetime supply of chicken from the poultry business he co-owns. Then he offered 40 to 50 thousand dollars to pay for a full-body tattoo. Luepke turned both down and asked for equity instead, and now he's a part owner of Greener Pastures Chicken. A backup fullback just became a share-holder in a future hall of famer’s company.

It was a great deal for Luepket. Luepke's opening offer was 2% of the company, and Miller said on his podcast that 2% would be worth "multiple hundreds of thousands of dollars." Work backward from that and the company is valued somewhere around 10 to 20 million dollars. Miller settled for giving up less than the full 2%, but even a sliver of a company that size is worth more than a tattoo or a freezer full of chicken, and unlike either of those, it can keep growing for the rest of Luepke's life. The chicken gets eaten in a year. The stake’s payout could come in 2040.

Equity is the right move here. Miller offered two things you consume and one thing you own, and the fullback took ownership. Most people, handed a perk, grab the perk, because free stuff feels like winning. The people who actually build wealth ask a different question when they have leverage: can I turn this into a piece of something instead of a one-time handout. Luepke had a jersey number a rich man wanted, and he converted that leverage into an asset instead of a treat.

But why is a jersey number worth this much to Miller in the first place. A number isn't just decor to top level NFL guys. It's identity. Miller wore 40 at DeSoto High School and at Texas A&M, where he actually majored in poultry science, which is how the chicken company exists at all. The number is his whole story in two digits, a Texas kid to a Super Bowl MVP. Players guard their numbers like names because that's basically what they are, and Miller wanted his origin story back badly enough to give up equity to get it.

So both men got the thing they valued most. Miller got the number that ties his career together, and Luepke got a piece of a business that could make more than his football contract. Miller called it the first jersey swap in NFL history done with ownership of a chicken farm, and he's probably right. He also handed a fullback a lesson every young player should copy: when someone with real money wants something you have, don't ask for a gift, ask for a share.

text:
Officer searched plates linked to his wife nearly 4,000 times before agency acted

A majority of Americans now oppose new data centers being built in their communities, and the opposition crosses party lines nearly evenly.

The Annenberg Public Policy Center surveyed 1,320 U.S. adults between June 16 and July 19, 2026, finding 61 percent opposed local data center construction, up from 49 percent months earlier. Sixty nine percent of Democrats, 54 percent of Republicans and 53 percent of independents opposed projects near them. Pew’s January 2026 survey found similar concerns centered on electricity costs, environmental effects and quality of life, though respondents were more likely to see positive than negative effects on local jobs and tax revenue.

The backlash has entered electoral politics. Reuters reported substantial opposition among Texas Republicans and Democrats alike, with residents citing utility costs, environmental strain and doubts about whether promised jobs offset resource demands.

As opposition has grown, some officials and tech investors have pointed to foreign influence. X reported identifying roughly 200 accounts tied to a suspected Chinese operation posting about U.S. AI, data center and energy policy. OpenAI had previously flagged China-origin accounts attempting to amplify existing concerns but found no evidence the effort achieved wide reach. 
WIRED and Axios both reported the underlying American opposition movement remains predominantly organic. President Trump has said communities without data centers risk becoming “backwards and poor,” framing construction as central to competition with China, according to AP.

Separately, networked surveillance infrastructure tied to license plate readers has drawn scrutiny. The ACLU reported that roughly 75 percent of police agencies using Flock cameras shared data nationally, with search records tied to immigration enforcement and a Texas abortion investigation. An analysis of 11.4 million searches over six months found more than 14 percent logged only as “investigation.”

A Washington Post investigation identified at least 69 police officials accused, charged or convicted of misusing license plate readers, including an Indianapolis officer who searched vehicles connected to his wife and acquaintances 3,759 times over ten months before the department suspended him. Florida has since banned local police license plate readers on state highways, and Texas paused state funding for Flock cameras. Reuters and Ipsos polling found 47 percent opposed such systems in their community, versus 38 percent in favor.

The EPA is now proposing to eliminate a federal requirement that states offer public notice and comment before issuing certain air pollution permits affecting data centers and other industrial facilities. States could still choose to provide those procedures, but would no longer be required to under federal rule.

🏍️💔 17-Year-Old Smithson Valley High School Student Killed in Comal County Motorcycle Crash 💔🏍️

Comal County, TX — A 17-year-old boy was killed Thursday morning in a crash involving a motorcycle and two pickup trucks on State Highway 46 near Stoney Creek Drive, east of Bulverde, according to the Texas Department of Public Safety.

DPS responded around 9 a.m. on September 3.

According to the preliminary investigation, the teenager was traveling westbound on SH 46 on a red Kawasaki Ninja when DPS said he failed to control his speed and crashed into a Ford pickup and a Chevrolet Silverado.

The teenager was ejected from the motorcycle and landed in a nearby ditch. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

DPS has not publicly identified the teenager. However, a letter obtained by KSAT identified him as a student at Smithson Valley High School.

School officials offered condolences to his family and said counseling and student support services are available for students, faculty and staff affected by the loss.

text:
Long post. Scroll on if you want. Stay if you still think this country’s worth saving.

You’re not wrong. Groceries, rent, insurance, gas — nobody feels like they’re winning right now. A lot of families are just trying to add a little more to the check so the month actually makes it.

That pain is real. The question is what caused it, and what happens if we forget.

Under Biden, gas went from about $2.40 to over $5 and never fully came back. A Harris continuation would’ve kept choking American energy. Trump declared an energy emergency on Day One, opened leasing, ended the LNG pause, and prices were heading toward the high-$2s by early 2026. Then the pump jumped again.

If he hadn’t done that first, this war-time spike would be horrific. He actually cares whether American families can eat and drive. He’s been working to keep costs down during a war. That matters.

The jump is Iran. Ugly. Not optional.

Iran spent years building a nuclear program, arming proxies, and holding a knife to the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint for about a fifth of the world’s oil. When they moved to shut that route and hit shipping, they weren’t protesting. They were trying to own the global energy tap and use it against the United States and our allies. A closed Strait under Iranian control would have made every grocery bill, freight bill, and farm bill worse for years. The war costs. Letting them lock that door would have cost more.

Yes, the Strait was open before the war. Open is not the same as safe. It was open because Iran allowed it — while they built the means to slam it shut. That’s not peace. That’s a hostage situation with tankers. Waiting until after they had a nuke and a locked chokepoint would have made this spike look cheap.

We’d already be further along on energy and that fight if Democrats weren’t blocking Trump at every turn. They magnify problems. They don’t offer real solutions. They want power.

Take Medicare for All. Sounds merciful. It comes with a chain. A federal system that size doesn’t just “help people.” It puts Washington in charge of doctors, hospitals, drugs, and the timing of care. That is centralized power. The Constitution separates power on purpose. A lot of the left hates that design. They already hold enormous soft power — media, campuses, bureaucracies, NGOs. Add a single national health payment system and you get constructive centralization without ever passing a constitutional amendment. Power moves to one center. That’s the point.

Get them back in and this doesn’t stay “high prices.” It becomes the on-ramp to communism. If this feels bad now, try living under that. That’s a real threat.

The spike is the war, not the plan collapsing. More oil is moving through the Strait again. Bypass routes are being built. The Venezuela deal just locked in a massive Western Hemisphere supply. Those barrels should bring prices back down.

Kitchen table first. Don’t let the ad war sell you amnesia.

text:
You step on a sheet of bond paper. Someone traces your feet. Then you wait.

In an age when shoes can be ordered with a few taps and delivered from factories thousands of kilometers away, Justin Neil along Recto in Manila still does things the old-fashioned way: shoes made to order, repaired by hand and designed to last for years.

Digital creator Hans Lawrence Malgapu recently put the spotlight on the shop in a Facebook post, calling it “relatively one of the institutions in the area” and recalling its reputation for customized shoes with soles made from airplane tires.

The owner’s sales pitch, according to Malgapu, was wonderfully straightforward: “Mauuna ka pa mapudpod kesa diyan.”

Malgapu says his own experience backs it up. His pair of brogues or spectators, bought in 2018, remains with him today.

“My pair of brogues/spectators has not only added to my style since 2018, but has also saved my life many times, especially during Habagat,” he wrote.

And Justin Neil isn’t merely repairing old shoes. Photos shared by Malgapu show rows of leather boots, brogues and cowboy boots in different shapes and finishes.

Getting a customized pair is refreshingly low-tech. Malgapu said customers simply step on bond paper and have the outline of their feet traced. Then they wait around three to five days for their shoes.

There is something almost defiant about that business model in 2026.

Fast fashion has trained consumers to buy cheaply, follow trends quickly and replace things just as quickly. Globalization and e-commerce have also given Filipinos easy access to inexpensive, factory-made footwear from around the world.

Yet shops like Justin Neil continue to survive because they offer something mass production struggles to replicate: customization, repairability and craftsmanship built around the individual customer.

Justin Neil also repairs worn-out footwear. Malgapu described bringing in shoes that have started to “talk”—when the soles begin separating after years of use—and having the shop’s craftsmen stitch them back together so they remain “shut.”

The shop carries other leather goods as well, including belts and wallets. Malgapu also noted what he described as snakeskin belts among its merchandise.

Justin Neil’s continued presence in Recto is a reminder that cheaper and faster do not always mean better.

Sometimes the answer to a worn-out shoe isn’t to throw it away and buy another pair.

Sometimes you take it back to a craftsman—and let it walk again.

(✍️ :Top Dagohoy)

text:
Many people point to today's China's superior material progress and call for some of the same in the US. The problem is that we lack the 5000+ history of China, during which various populations were amalgamated into a common identity-consciousness,  as a "Chinese civilization" with at its heartland  a Han civilization. China through the millennia naturally and organically expanded into its hinterlands and interlands to form what it is today, to include Taiwan.   
     By economic necessity, in the 400+ years since their first arrival from Great Britain, the first-comers forced in,  invited in, or absorbed, mostly  inorganically and unnaturally from outside the hemisphere,  vast numbers of the most diverse populations. You want to know how they feel about them?    I offer you the words of judge Leon M. Bazile of the Caroline County Circuit Court in Virginia, in his written opinion of January 22, 1965 , in which he refused to vacate Richard and Mildred Loving’s 1959 convictions under Virginia’s ban on interracial marriage:“Almighty God created the races white, black, yellow, malay and red, and he placed them on separate continents. And but for the interference with his arrangement there would be no cause for such marriages."  We are not speaking of ancient history  here.  In 1965 young republicans were graduating from Virginia's law schools, fully in accord with Judge Belize's attitudes and opinions. Today they are the judges that Virginians from all those colored races have to face. especially in the courts in the 20th Circuit Court of Virginia. From that reality,  try to imagine the future history of the "great civilization" of the United States.
     At the same we can read  in our common spaces, that the Hispanic civilization in the Americas is one of the longest, most continuous civilizational projects in the Hemisphere — 533 years from 1492 to today. It is not just "Spanish rule" but the transplantation and evolution of a complete society. At its peak around 1790, the Hispanic world controlled directly about 2/3 of the entire American Hemisphere from claims in Alaska down the entire west coast and the  south-western states we all know having belonged to Spain, down to the southernmost Cape Horn in Chile. And if one speaks of a Latin (Catholic) civilization, to include Brazil. Thus we are led to the conclusion that while political independence broke the administrative unity, it did not break the civilizational unity. That is why the concept of La Hispanidad or Hispanic America persists: it describes a community that shares language, faith, law, urban form, and family structure, stretching over 10,000 km north to south, even when it speaks with 20 different political voices.
     Quo Vadis? Then the unasked question is:  which civilization is closer to the requirements of territoriality and commonality for a "great civilization" to compete with China or even Russia: an "Anglo-Saxon" America or a Hispanic America? Or rather,  does logic require that it be an amalgamation of the two?

text:
⚡️The deeper fracture is that young people are beginning to realize the old bargain may no longer exist.

For most of modern life, society offered a simple deal:

Become useful.
Build skills.
Work hard.
Climb.
Trade your labor for security.

AI attacks the foundation of that bargain because it attacks the scarcity of the labor itself.

A person can spend ten years becoming excellent at analysis, coding, law, finance, design, writing, research, coordination, and then watch the economic value of that expertise compress because cognition became reproducible.

That realization changes something psychologically before unemployment ever explodes.

You stop believing the institution will protect the years you give it.

And once that belief dies, career loyalty dies with it.

Why sacrifice your twenties proving yourself to a corporation that may discover at 38 that three people plus agents can do what your department used to do?

Why build your identity around professional competence when competence itself is becoming cheaper?

Why defer your life for a ladder whose upper rungs may disappear before you reach them?

That is the signal inside the 73%.

The young are beginning to sense that human usefulness may no longer guarantee human security.

That is historically enormous.

Because employment has carried far more than income.

It gave people status.

Routine.

Community.

Identity.

A reason to wake up.

A path into adulthood.

A way to prove value.

AI therefore threatens something deeper than payroll.

It threatens the social mechanism through which millions of people were told they would earn a place in the world.

And this is where the pressure becomes political.

If output keeps rising while fewer human hours are required, the question becomes unavoidable:

Who owns the productivity?

If the answer is mostly shareholders, founders, infrastructure owners, and capital, while everyone else competes for a shrinking pool of valuable labor, the system becomes unstable.

People will demand another claim on the machine.

Ownership.

Dividends.

Transfers.

Public capital funds.

Reduced working time.

Something.

Because a civilization cannot indefinitely tell people:

“Your economic worth comes from your labor”

while simultaneously building machines whose purpose is to make that labor less necessary.

That contradiction eventually breaks.

And the deepest cultural consequence may be even larger.

For centuries, work answered the question:

What are you for?

AI is beginning to weaken that answer.

If machines eventually outperform humans across enormous portions of economically useful cognition, people will be forced back toward an older and harder question:

What is a human life for when usefulness is no longer the price of admission?

That question leads straight into everything we were discussing about meaning.

Family.

Creation.

Service.

Truth.

Community.

Love.

Exploration.

Faith.

Responsibility.

Things whose value does not disappear because a machine can perform them more efficiently.

So the deepest transition may ultimately be brutal and liberating at the same time.

Human beings spent the industrial age proving their worth through production.

AI may force civilization to discover whether human worth survives after production stops being uniquely human.

text:
The Dead Sea Scrolls are among the greatest archaeological discoveries of the twentieth century. Found in caves near the Dead Sea between 1947 and 1956, the collection transformed historians' understanding of the Hebrew Bible, ancient Judaism, and the world into which Christianity emerged.

The first scrolls were discovered by Bedouin shepherds in caves near Qumran. Archaeologists later excavated the surrounding area and uncovered thousands of manuscript fragments representing hundreds of separate texts. Written primarily in Hebrew, with some in Aramaic and Greek, the scrolls date from roughly the third century BC to the first century AD.

Among the discoveries were some of the oldest surviving copies of books from the Hebrew Bible, predating previously known manuscripts by nearly a thousand years. The remarkable agreement between these ancient texts and later copies demonstrated how carefully biblical writings had been preserved over the centuries, while also revealing small variations that have helped scholars better understand how the scriptures were transmitted and edited over time.

The scrolls include far more than biblical manuscripts. They contain religious commentaries, legal texts, hymns, prayers, calendars, and community rules that provide an extraordinary glimpse into Jewish life during the Second Temple period. Together, they reveal a diverse religious landscape with multiple groups holding different beliefs and practices before the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 AD.

Because the scrolls date to the same era in which Christianity first emerged, they have also become invaluable to historians studying the origins of both Judaism and Christianity. They offer important context for understanding the religious ideas, traditions, and expectations that shaped the world of the New Testament.

text:
Jesus’ church today is the body of Christ:

All who repent and believe the gospel He and His apostles delivered, gathered in local congregations that preach that gospel, baptize, and remember His death until He comes. It is not a single 19th-century corporation with a living prophet, extra scriptures, restored priesthood keys, and temple ordinances unknown to the New Testament. It is the same church He founded, still built on the apostles and prophets with Christ Himself as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), not rebuilt after a claimed total apostasy.

Who founded it? Jesus Christ. He said He would build His church and the gates of hell would not prevail against it. That promise does not require a 1,700-year total collapse followed by a farm-boy prophet, golden plates, and angelic priesthood restorations that left no contemporary public evidence.

Who authorized it? The same Jesus who commissioned the original apostles as eyewitnesses of His resurrection. That office was unique and foundational (Ephesians 2:20). It is not a rotating corporate board that needs replenishing every time a member dies. Claiming Peter, James, and John appeared in 1829 to confer Melchizedek priesthood is an extra-biblical assertion that stands or falls on Joseph Smith’s word, not on the New Testament pattern.

Where are its apostles? They finished their work. The church is built on that foundation, not still waiting for a new Quorum of the Twelve to issue policy letters and settle every doctrinal shift. Living “apostles” who were not eyewitnesses of the risen Christ are a different office wearing the same title.

Who settles doctrine? The apostolic teaching already given and written. Scripture plus the historic rule of faith the early church used to reject later innovations. A living prophet who can revise previous revelations, introduce new ordinances, and change temple rites is convenient for an organization. It is not how the New Testament describes the once-for-all faith.

What happens to the dead and the unreached? God judges justly. He is not dependent on 21st-century temple work and proxy baptisms to offer people a chance He somehow forgot to give them.

In 1 Corinthians 15:29 Paul is arguing for the resurrection, not installing a new ordinance. Some people were being “baptized for the dead.” Paul does not command the practice, explain how to do it, or assign it to the church. He uses it as a reductio: if the dead are not raised at all, that practice is pointless, so even they assume the dead rise. The logic is “your own custom refutes your denial of resurrection,” not “go start vicarious baptisms.” People are saved by grace through faith in Christ, not by later rituals performed in their name.

The only book with a paper trail that actually exists is the Bible.The New Testament sits on more than 5,700 catalogued Greek manuscripts, plus more than 10,000 Latin copies and thousands more in Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Georgian, Ethiopic, and other ancient languages. Combined New Testament witnesses routinely exceed 24,000. Fragments reach into the second century, within living memory of the apostles.

The Old Testament is backed by the Masoretic tradition, the Septuagint, and the Dead Sea Scrolls, which put Isaiah and other books a thousand years closer to the originals than the medieval copies we already had. That is a mountain of physical, datable, publicly examined copies.

The Book of Mormon has zero ancient manuscripts. No Reformed Egyptian text. No gold plates available for inspection. No chain of copies spanning centuries. Joseph Smith dictated an English book in 1829. The plates, we are told, went back to an angel. What remains are 19th-century handwritten English manuscripts of that dictation, not ancient witnesses of an ancient record. Witness statements are not manuscripts. A missing artifact is not a textual tradition.

You ask for blueprints - Those are the original ones. The Bible has thousands of them, in multiple languages, from multiple centuries, sitting in libraries and museums. Joseph Smith’s additional scripture has none. The LDS system adds another god, another Christology, another priesthood, another set of saving ordinances, and another canon.

That is not the church Jesus founded. It is a later reconstruction that revises the Bible-based gospel. Sincere members are not the issue. The claims are. The test is whether the foundation is the transmitted apostolic record or a restoration story that begins and ends with one man’s word.

text:
From @mijalbitton
The Problem is that Nessel Makes Sense 
parshat  Nitzavim, Politics, and the Fight over Jewish Survival 

When Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel got up in front of a room of Jewish Democrats last weekend and told them they may need to sacrifice the safety, and even the future, of their own people in exchange for saving the rest of humanity, many of us were shocked, and for good reason.

Her words brought to mind the European Jews a century ago who told their fellow Jews to stop advocating against antisemitism because it hurt their country.

According to news reports, Nessel reached for Queen Esther as the model, saying it might now be up to Jewish Democrats to follow in Esther’s path. But that is the Purim story turned inside out. Esther did not sacrifice the Jews for a greater good. She sacrificed herself for the Jews. To recruit her as the patron saint of setting Jewish safety aside is to get the story grotesquely backward.

But being shocked lets us off the hook. What Nessel said was not a slip. Inside a certain logic, she makes sense.

A week earlier she had reiterated her concerns over Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee, focusing on the excuses he offered after Temple Israel synagogue and its preschool outside Detroit were attacked. Now she appeared to be preparing to support him, or at least to stand out of his way, and she seemed to be reaching for vocabulary that would make this justifiable on Jewish grounds.

What we must understand is that in doing so, Nessel drew on a way of thinking that has been common in parts of American liberal Judaism for decades. The idea is that Jewish survival is not really a value at all but an interest, and when interests conflict with values, values are supposed to win.

In my early twenties, I discovered American liberal Judaism. I already knew traditional, Orthodox, Sephardic, familial Judaism like the back of my hand. This new one was a whole world, and there was a lot in it I came to love: its seriousness about ethics and its unselfconscious confidence in engaging with the wider culture.

The longer I stayed, the more I realized it had, even if it wouldn't always admit it, its own sacred cows and orthodoxies. What surprised me most was that the fights weren't only about practice or politics. They were about what counted as a Jewish value in the first place.

Back then, the hot conversations were about intermarriage and assimilation, fought largely through the population studies sociologists were producing.

As a sociologist and community builder, I had to take a side. I felt strongly that giving up on valuing Jews marrying Jews as a value was wrong. That didn’t mean we couldn’t include Jews who had made other choices. It meant that a community has the right and the responsibility to articulate an ideal: that a Jew who cares about Judaism should want a partner who cares about it too. Democrats want to marry Democrats. Nobody thinks that’s bigotry.

1/

text:
Jesus’ church today is the body of Christ: all who repent and believe the gospel He and His apostles delivered, gathered in local congregations that preach that gospel, baptize, and remember His death until He comes.

It is not a single 19th-century corporation with a living prophet, extra scriptures, restored priesthood keys, and temple ordinances unknown to the New Testament. It is the same church He founded, still built on the apostles and prophets with Christ Himself as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), not rebuilt after a claimed total apostasy.

Who founded it? Jesus Christ. He said He would build His church and the gates of hell would not prevail against it. That promise does not require a 1,700-year total collapse followed by a farm-boy prophet, golden plates, and angelic priesthood restorations that left no contemporary public evidence.

Who authorized it? The same Jesus who commissioned the original apostles as eyewitnesses of His resurrection. That office was unique and foundational (Ephesians 2:20). It is not a rotating corporate board that needs replenishing every time a member dies. 

Claiming Peter, James, and John appeared in 1829 to confer Melchizedek priesthood is an extra-biblical assertion that stands or falls on Joseph Smith’s word, not on the New Testament pattern.

Where are its apostles? They finished their work. The church is built on that foundation, not still waiting for a new Quorum of the Twelve to issue policy letters and settle every doctrinal shift.

Living “apostles” who were not eyewitnesses of the risen Christ are a different office wearing the same title.

Who settles doctrine? The apostolic teaching already given and written. Scripture plus the historic rule of faith the early church used to reject later innovations. A living prophet who can revise previous revelations, introduce new ordinances, and change temple rites is convenient for an organization. It is not how the New Testament describes the once-for-all faith.

What happens to the dead and the unreached? God judges justly. He is not dependent on 21st-century temple work and proxy baptisms to offer people a chance He somehow forgot to give them.

In 1 Corinthians 15:29 Paul is arguing for the resurrection, not installing a new ordinance. Some people were being “baptized for the dead.” Paul does not command the practice, explain how to do it, or assign it to the church. He uses it as a reductio: if the dead are not raised at all, that practice is pointless, so even they assume the dead rise. The logic is “your own custom refutes your denial of resurrection,” not “go start vicarious baptisms.” People are saved by grace through faith in Christ, not by later rituals performed in their name.

The only book with a paper trail that actually exists is the Bible. The New Testament sits on more than 5,700 catalogued Greek manuscripts, plus more than 10,000 Latin copies and thousands more in Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Georgian, Ethiopic, and other ancient languages. Combined New Testament witnesses routinely exceed 24,000. Fragments reach into the second century, within living memory of the apostles. 

The Old Testament is backed by the Masoretic tradition, the Septuagint, and the Dead Sea Scrolls, which put Isaiah and other books a thousand years closer to the originals than the medieval copies we already had. That is a mountain of physical, datable, publicly examined copies.

The Book of Mormon has zero ancient manuscripts. No Reformed Egyptian text. No gold plates available for inspection. No chain of copies spanning centuries. Joseph Smith dictated an English book in 1829. The plates, we are told, went back to an angel. What remains are 19th-century handwritten English manuscripts of that dictation, not ancient witnesses of an ancient record.

Witness statements are not manuscripts. A missing artifact is not a textual tradition.

You asked for blueprints. Those are the original ones. The Bible has thousands of them, in multiple languages, from multiple centuries, sitting in libraries and museums. Joseph Smith’s additional scripture has none. 

The LDS system adds another god, another Christology, another priesthood, another set of saving ordinances, and another canon. That is not the church Jesus founded.

It is a later reconstruction that revises the Bible-based gospel. Sincere members are not the issue. The claims are. The test is whether the foundation is the transmitted apostolic record or a restoration story that begins and ends with one man’s word.

text:
You’re measuring 78 years of intent with three post-7 October items. That is not how intent is measured. Intent over the life of the conflict is measured by who accepted partition when it was offered, who answered recognition with war, and who walked away from maps that already created a Palestinian state.
1. The founding vote went the other way.
November 1947: UNGA 181 recommended two states. The Jewish Agency accepted a truncated Jewish state. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab League rejected any Jewish sovereignty and chose war. Five Arab armies invaded in May 1948. That is the original “never” vote. It was not an Israeli parliament voting against a Palestinian state. It was Arab governments voting, with armies, against a Jewish one.
2. After 1967, the official Arab position was explicit.
September 1967, Khartoum: “no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with Israel.” That is a collective Arab League resolution, not a tweet. Israel had just taken the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan and was signalling land-for-peace. The answer was three nos.
3. When Palestinian institutions finally voted, they voted to drop destruction language — then Hamas reversed the politics.
April 1996: the PLO’s Palestine National Council voted 504–54 to cancel the charter clauses calling for Israel’s destruction. That is the closest thing to a Palestinian parliamentary vote on Israel’s existence. It went toward recognition, under Oslo. Hamas never accepted that bargain. In 2006 it won the last PLC election and refused the Quartet conditions: recognize Israel, accept prior agreements, renounce violence. There has been no functioning Palestinian parliament since. You cannot demand a 68–9 Palestinian counter-vote from a legislature that Hamas froze, and Abbas never reconvened.
4. The “Israel never offered a state” claim is false.

Camp David 2000 / Clinton Parameters Dec 2000: Palestinian state on ~94–97% of the West Bank plus Gaza, land swaps, capital in Arab East Jerusalem, limited refugee return to Israel. Barak accepted the parameters as a basis; Arafat did not. Clinton said so at the time.
Olmert 2008: ~93.7% of the West Bank plus swaps to ~99.7% equivalent, Gaza–West Bank link, shared Jerusalem arrangements. Abbas did not accept and later said he never studied the map. No counter-offer.

Those are not adjectives. They are maps. The Palestinian leadership did not sign them.
5. Gaza 2005 is the control experiment.
Israel withdrew every settler and soldier from Gaza. It did not get a peaceful proto-state. It got Hamas rule, rockets, and 7 October. That is why a 2024 Knesset that lived through the massacre voted 68–9 against repeating the experiment “west of the Jordan,” including as part of a deal. That vote is a reaction to a massacre, not the origin of the conflict.
6. What the three items actually are.

July 2024 Knesset text: a non-binding declaration, 68–9. Netanyahu did not vote. Yesh Atid walked out. Only Arab lists voted no. It does not repeal Oslo, does not annex the West Bank, and does not bind the next Knesset.
September 2025 Netanyahu at E1: a coalition prime minister stating current policy after 7 October and after a wave of Western recognitions that Israel reads as a prize for Hamas.
August 2026 E1 tenders: settlement policy designed, as Smotrich said when the plans were approved, to make a contiguous Palestinian state harder. That is real, and it is late. It does not erase 1947, 1967, 2000 or 2008.

7. The Palestinian parliament question is a category error.
No Palestinian parliament ever voted 68–9 to “rule out a state for Israel” because the maximalist position was already in the 1964/68 PLO charter and the 1988 Hamas charter. The one large PLO vote on the books removed destruction language. Hamas never ratified that removal. Polls still show a split: generic “two states” often loses or barely wins; a detailed 1967-line package does better in some PCPSR waves, while majorities often say two states is no longer practical and oppose Hamas disarmament. That is public opinion, not a parliament.
The actual sequence
1947: Jews accept partition, Arabs reject and go to war.
1967: Arab League formalizes no peace / no recognition / no talks.
1993–96: PLO recognizes Israel on paper; PNC amends the charter.
2000 and 2008: Israeli governments put statehood maps on the table; Palestinian leaders do not close.
2005: Israel leaves Gaza; Hamas takes it.
2006: last Palestinian election puts Hamas in the PLC; no recognition of Israel follows.
2023: 7 October.
2024–26: an Israeli right-religious coalition says, in votes and concrete, that it will not create a sovereign Palestinian state next door after that massacre.

If your test of “wanted peace” is only whether today’s Knesset still endorses a Palestinian state after 7 October, you have defined the test so that the answer is automatic. If the test is who accepted a Jewish state when it was first offered, and who later walked away from Palestinian statehood maps, the record does not start in July 2024.

Intent is measured in those votes too — the 1947 acceptance, the Khartoum nos, the 1996 PNC amendment, the unsigned 2000 and 2008 maps — not only in three items chosen from the two years after the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust.

I once worked a 3 month contract in Atlanta. I stayed 12 miles from the office and I had to leave by 5:50am if I wanted to make sure to be at work by 8am. 
I moved to just over 4 miles directly downtown the road the office was on and it still took me 45 minutes to get there. 
At the end of the contract, they offered me a full time position. I asked if I could work remotely and stay living in Florida. They told me no, I’d have to relocate and work in the office 5 days a week.  I told them that they couldn’t pay me enough to live in Atlanta. They said I shouldn’t be so sure and they wanted me to name a number. I told them that if they offered a minimum of $250,000 a year and 10 weeks of PTO, I’d start to THINK about considering it. They couldn’t do that and I basically said, “told you so.”  And as I thought about it, $250K wouodnt have been enough anyway. I just threw out a number because they asked me to. 
I liked the people there and I liked the job okay…but there’s no way I’d live and drive daily in Atlanta.

text:
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth recently posted an image mocking Canada’s Cadet Training. His petty body shaming insult should be rejected, but the Cadets are a powerful tool for drawing teens into reactionary militarism.

To familiarize young people with the Canadian Forces (CF) the military spends more than $300 million a year on the Royal Canadian Sea Cadets, Royal Canadian Army Cadets and Royal Canadian Air Cadets. The largest and oldest government-funded youth program, over 50,000 kids are part of the free afterschool initiative. Participants may receive school credits and the government offers up hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in post-secondary scholarships to cadets. 

They sometimes also receive cash bonuses for attending. According to the Canadian Forces’ description, “it is a national program for young Canadians aged 12 to 18 who are interested in participating in a variety of fun, challenging and rewarding activities while learning about the Sea, Army and Air activities of the Canadian Armed Forces.” Nine- to 12-year-olds are also eligible for the Navy League Cadets.

The National Defence Act authorizes the minister to establish cadet chapters. Serving personnel, reservists and individuals given a military commission train the cadets. Part of the CF Reserve, the Cadet Instructors Cadre is the largest officer branch in the CF.

Military officials say the program is designed to teach teens how to become good citizens, but cadets learn about the CF’s procedures and traditions and are taught to appreciate its emblems and symbols. According to an official description, one aim of the cadets is “to stimulate the interest of youth in the sea, land, and air activities of the Canadian Forces.”

The program instils reverence for warfare. Cadets often attend Remembrance Day celebrations and other military commemorations. “Growing up as a Canadian cadet,” explains Kelly Jarman in “The Cost of Canada’s Militarist Culture: Perspectives From a Former Cadet”, “I was taught that the military is the most important aspect of society and that it deserves unquestioned respect. Trips to museums, Remembrance Day parades and even school assignments were all designed to instill in us the idea that soldiers are noble and that wars are fought for democracy and freedom. The very idea of citizenship is linked to military culture, something that became evident when we toured the HMCS Fredericton naval war ship during a so-called ‘Citizenship Trip.’”

The cadet program develops obedient soldiers rather than politically active citizens. Participants are subject to the military’s hierarchal rank system. The CF boasts that cadets “develop a great
sense of pride and discipline through their involvement in a hierarchical system that allows them to hone their leadership skills as they grow older and they learn to care for younger cadets.”

Along with socializing members into its rank system, cadets can learn marksmanship, parachuting and other military skills. Much of the training takes place at summer camps on bases. Historically, the base training simulated warlike scenarios. In a horrific training mishap, six teens died and dozens were injured when a live grenade exploded at a cadet camp in Valcartier, QC, in 1974.

The cadets began as a paramilitary group explicitly designed to prepare youth for war. The first “drill association” was set up to train boys to fight in 1861. Expanding its support to schools providing military training, Ottawa issued a Militia General Order that authorized the formation of 74 “Associations for Drill in Educational Institutions” in 1879. Two decades later Ontario granted $50 ($1,500 today) to schools with more than 25 boys in the cadets. In 1908 the Department of Militia and Defence provided instructors, arms, books and exams to school-age males to standardize the different cadet training programs in Ontario and Québec secondary schools.

Conflict spurred drill activity. The 1860-65 US Civil War, 1866– 67 Fenian Raids, 1869–70 Red River Rebellion and 1885 Northwest Rebellion sparked interest in “drill associations”. During WWI 64,000 children were in the Cadet Corps. Some 40,000 former cadets fought in the First World War.

Girls weren’t officially admitted to the cadets until the 1970s. In 1975 Parliament changed the word “boys” to “persons” in the cadet legislation. But patriarchy dies hard. Controversy erupted in 2016 over a code-of-conduct pamphlet given to cadets that referred to the four Bs — “boobs, belly, bums, boxers”. In what some viewed as shaming female cadets, the pamphlet said girls should not wear shirts that “reveal their developing bits” (breasts).

A series of reports suggest that sexual abuse is a problem in the organization. In 2016 VICE News “obtained documents that prove that the Canadian Forces’ cadet program has grappled with hundreds of cases of sexual assault, harassment, discrimination, and abuse” over the decades.

In 2006 Ottawa agreed to pay $8 million to 35 former sea cadets who were sexually assaulted. Several other sexual abuse lawsuits are pending. A suit launched in 2016 from former cadets in the Atlantic provinces alleged the organization created an environment “which encouraged or fostered silence and obedience” when abuse took place. Some suggest that abusers are attracted to cadet training positions since it puts them in contact with children and the hierarchical structure — having to obey commanding officers — enables abuse.

Young Canadians deserve better than the Cadets.

text:
⚠️ 🇺🇸 RFK Jr.'s Military Vaccine Probe Threatens Public Health Gains as Evidence Confirms Shots Saved Millions

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is using an Army doctor with a record of disputed claims to hunt for hidden COVID-19 vaccine deaths among troops, even as peer-reviewed studies show the vaccines averted millions of deaths and high-quality respirators remain the most reliable individual defense against ongoing airborne transmission.

An Army flight surgeon now advising both Kennedy and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a federal court she is examining more than 2,500 unverified VAERS reports of service-member deaths and claims she personally knows of 28 vaccine-related fatalities. Theresa Long, assigned as Kennedy's senior medical military adviser shortly before her planned retirement, has spent years alleging the 2021 Biden-era mandate caused widespread myocarditis, cancer and other injuries that the Pentagon covered up. A 2026 Politico report based on her August deposition describes the work as part of a broader look at whether government surveillance systems hid vaccine harms. The Defense Department has not confirmed the details of her current assignment and instead points to its ongoing effort to reinstate troops discharged for refusing the shots.

Those claims collide with the weight of the evidence. A 2025 JAMA Health Forum analysis estimated COVID-19 vaccination prevented 2.5 million deaths worldwide between 2020 and 2024, with a sensitivity range of 1.4 million to 4 million. Most of the benefit accrued to older adults. Updated shots continue to reduce hospitalizations; a 2026 JAMA review found vaccine effectiveness against hospitalization of 53 percent among adults 65 and older in the most recent season and no new safety signals. Myocarditis after mRNA vaccination occurs, mainly in young men, at roughly 27 cases per million in the first week, according to FDA labeling. Infection itself produces higher rates of the same heart inflammation and other cardiac events, a pattern confirmed in Pentagon data that showed the post-vaccination rise was short-lived.

Long's earlier reliance on Defense Medical Epidemiology Database spikes was later attributed by the Pentagon to a tabulation error in pre-pandemic baselines, a finding corroborated by contemporaneous fact-checks. Kennedy has already overhauled the CDC's vaccine advisory committee, scaled back childhood recommendations and ended routine COVID shots for most healthy Americans. Uptake among adults has fallen into the high teens. Public-health groups this week again urged vaccination for those at risk of severe disease.

SARS-CoV-2 remains an airborne pathogen. Well-fitted N95, KN95, FFP2 or P100 respirators filter at least 95 percent of the smallest infectious particles and offer far more protection than cloth or loose surgical masks in shared indoor air. Communities that treat high-quality respirators as routine infrastructure, rather than optional extras, reduce both acute illness and the long-term burden of repeated infections.

Kennedy's investigation may satisfy those who view every mandate as an abuse of power. Treating rare, already-acknowledged side effects as proof of a vast cover-up, however, risks further eroding confidence in tools that demonstrably cut deaths and hospitalizations. Service members and civilians still face a circulating virus. Vaccines remain safe and effective for those who need them. Respirators work every day. The data, not the latest inquiry, should guide policy.

text:
I normally treat Trump’s Truth Social posts as noise from a badly behaved child; something to be ignored because his stream-of-consciousness griping and rambling are endless and toxic. But his latest post annoys me no end.

Trump now says he intends to ask European countries to reimburse the United States for military aid and munitions previously provided to Ukraine, claiming that Europe would have paid for them if the Biden administration had simply asked. What he says is largely nonsense and not worth the bytes of storage it consumes. But I am refuting it anyway because I am a good girl.

Firstly, Trump is profoundly misguided. Europe does not owe the United States anything. Congress appropriated American assistance to Ukraine in pursuit of American foreign-policy and national-security objectives (with substantial Republican support). European governments were not parties to some uncollected debt that Trump can now retroactively decide exists.

Secondly, “hundreds of billions” simply did not disappear into Ukraine. A substantial portion of U.S. spending associated with the war was spent in the United States, including replenishing American weapons stocks, purchasing equipment from American manufacturers, and supporting the U.S. military presence in Europe.

Thirdly, European countries have spent enormous sums of their own supporting Ukraine, accepting refugees, expanding their militaries, and strengthening NATO's eastern flank.

Lastly, it is ironic that Trump is complaining about depleted American munitions in the same statement. Whatever strains Ukraine placed on particular U.S. inventories, his own war of choice with Iran has consumed large quantities of precisely the weapons the United States needs for other contingencies. Reuters reported last month that the U.S. Army had used up much of its global stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles, with sources saying it had expended "virtually all" of its ATACMS and PrSM inventory during the Iran war. U.S. military leaders had also warned Trump about dwindling stocks of defensive weapons, including Patriot interceptors. If Trump wants to complain about depleted American arsenals, he should start with the war he chose to fight.

European leaders should offer Trump their metaphorical middle finger, as Canada did. Treat Trump with the ridicule he deserves.

text:
WHAT DID THEY GET?

The tree isn't called:

Tree of Evil.

It's called:

Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil.

And “knowing good and evil” has several possible meanings in biblical Hebrew.

This has been debated for decades.

Scholarly proposals include:

moral discernment

wisdom

maturity

comprehensive knowledge

sexual maturity

autonomous decision-making

and even:

authority to administer judgment/reward and punishment.

I can actually test some of these against other biblical passages.

Children DON'T “know good and evil”

Deuteronomy 1:39 describes:

“…your children, which in that day had no knowledge between good and evil…”

That strongly suggests the phrase can describe mature discernment.

Children don't possess it.

Adults do.

That's important.

An elderly man can LOSE the ability

2 Samuel 19:35 has the elderly Barzillai ask:

“can I discern between good and evil?”

Again, this sounds like:

judgment

discernment

mental capacity

rather than simply:

“I know sin exists.”

And then Solomon gives us a huge clue

Solomon asks for wisdom to govern.

1 Kings 3:9:

“Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad…”

God approves the request.

This is extremely important because it proves:

The ability to distinguish good and evil is NOT inherently sinful.

God gives Solomon precisely that ability.

One scholarly interpretation therefore argues that Genesis isn't condemning wisdom itself; the problem is humanity seizing wisdom independently rather than receiving it properly within relationship to God.

So perhaps the problem wasn't KNOWLEDGE

This is where the story changes.

The traditional simplified version is:

God didn't want humans to know things.

But that's difficult to sustain.

Genesis already portrays humans as intelligent.

Adam names animals.

Humans are given responsibility over creation.

And elsewhere God gives wisdom.

The issue may instead concern:

crossing a boundary to acquire a divine prerogative independently.

That fits Genesis 3:6 particularly well.

Eve sees that the tree was:

“a tree to be desired to make one wise…”

So wisdom is explicitly part of the narrative.

Nathan French's detailed 2021 study argues that “knowledge of good and evil” concerns the knowledge required for administering reward and punishment—in other words, a kind of judicial authority associated with divine rule.

And his argument specifically observes that Genesis 3:5 and 3:22 associate this knowledge with God/divine beings.

If that interpretation is right, the serpent isn't merely saying:

“Eat this and you'll learn right from wrong.”

It is offering something closer to:

You will acquire a capacity associated with divine authority and judgment.

That changes the story considerably.

But this is my scholarly interpretation, not something we can declare settled.

Now go back to the serpent's promise

Genesis 3:5:

“your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.”

Then:

Genesis 3:7:

“the eyes of them both were opened”

Then:

Genesis 3:22:

“the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil.”

Look at the structure.

SERPENT PREDICTS:

Eyes opened

↓

Like divine beings

↓

Knowing good and evil

NARRATIVE REPORTS:

Eyes opened

↓

DIVINE SPEAKER CONFIRMS:

Human became like one of us

Knowing good and evil

That parallel is real.

“The serpent simply lied about everything.”

But the serpent leaves something out

This may be the trick.

The serpent emphasizes what humanity will gain.

knowledge

opened eyes

divine likeness

But doesn't explain what humanity will lose.

After eating:

knowledge acquired

↓

eyes opened

↓

human becomes “like one of us”

BUT

↓

shame

↓

alienation

↓

judgment

↓

expulsion

↓

Tree of Life blocked

↓

mortality.

So perhaps the deception wasn't primarily:

“Nothing I told you will happen.”

It may have been:

“I told you what you would gain without telling you the true cost.”

That's an inference—but it fits the narrative surprisingly well.

And notice: there were TWO trees

This may be the biggest clue.

Genesis has:

TREE 1

Knowledge of Good and Evil

and

TREE 2

Tree of Life

After humanity acquires the first, the divine speaker says:

“Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life… and live for ever…”

This suggests two distinct divine-like attributes:

KNOWLEDGE/WISDOM

and

IMMORTAL LIFE.

Humanity has obtained one.

It must now be prevented from obtaining the other.

That is right there in Genesis.

That means Eden's crisis can be read as a boundary crisis

Before:

HUMAN

has life dependent upon God

but lacks divine “knowledge of good and evil.”

Then:

SERPENT

↓

offers forbidden knowledge.

↓

HUMAN ACQUIRES IT

↓

Divine statement:

“has become like one of us.”

But then:

TREE OF LIFE BLOCKED

because otherwise humanity could:

eat

↓

live forever.

So Genesis appears concerned with the boundary between:

HUMAN

and

DIVINE.

That's much stronger textually than saying the fruit itself magically created evil.

And this connects to something MUCH bigger in Genesis 1–11

Watch the repeated pattern.

EDEN

Humans cross a divine boundary.

↓

Expelled.

GENESIS 6

“Sons of God” and human women cross another boundary.

↓

Nephilim / judgment / Flood.

BABEL

Humanity says:

“let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven…”

↓

Divine response:

“let us go down…”

↓

Humanity scattered.

Whether every one of these episodes should be interpreted identically is debatable.

But Genesis 1–11 repeatedly concerns boundaries between heaven and Earth, divine and human, permitted and forbidden power.

That deserves serious attention.

Eden may involve knowledge crossing from the divine sphere into humanity. Genesis 6/1 Enoch involves heavenly beings transferring forbidden knowledge to humanity.

That does not prove they are the same event or the same rebellion.

text:
HOKA GREW 19.8%. A YEAR LATER, 7.7%. THAT IS THE ONLY REASON DECKERS $DECK LOOKS CHEAP:

Deckers Outdoor DECK at $84.33 (after hours), after finishing the regular day at $84.50, +$0.74 / +0.88%. Six ways of looking at this market, and tonight they agree on something awkward: almost nothing well known is on sale. The growth board is nearly all small regional banks. The income board leads with shipping owners and life insurers. The famous names on the quality board cost about what they are worth. The one widely owned consumer brand carrying a real discount across all six is Deckers, and it is only there because its growth rate halved in twelve months.

The Goleta, California company owns HOKA running shoes and UGG boots. Same June quarter, one year apart. July 24, 2025: HOKA $653.1M, +19.8%; UGG $265.1M, +18.9%; total $964.5M, +16.9%. July 23, 2026: HOKA $703.5M, +7.7%; UGG $278.0M, +4.9%; total $1.020B, +5.7% - the first billion-dollar opening quarter in company history, at under half the growth rate. Profit did worse than sales: gross margin, what is left of each sales dollar after making the shoes, rose to 56.4% from 55.8%, and operating income still FELL, $155.3M against $165.3M. Per-share profit was $0.94 versus $0.93 - flat, and positive only because there are fewer shares to divide by.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
- HeartFlow at $50.00 (after hours), after finishing the regular day at $49.71, -$0.29 / -0.58%. The Mountain View company runs an ordinary CT heart scan through software that judges whether a narrowed artery is really restricting blood flow - the question that otherwise needs a catheter. This style watches a price climbing near its twelve-month best, and this is the steadiest such climb on the board: a high of $51.778 set yesterday, up from $20.13 on February 13. Company news sits under it - the August 13 quarter put revenue at $64.1M, +48%, and raised the full-year map to $246M-$250M from $228M-$232M. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: the high failing to hold, or November's report walking that raise back. Verdict: a real climb on its own figures, at a business still losing money and priced near 17 times a full year of expected revenue.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
- Procter & Gamble at $147.06 (after hours), after finishing the regular day at $146.92, -$0.72 / -0.49%. Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest. This style wants a durable business at a fair price. Durable is as settled as it gets - shelf space in nearly every supermarket on earth. Price is the whole argument. From the July 29 full-year report: organic sales, which strip out currency and businesses bought or sold, grew 1% across the year, all of it from charging more rather than selling more. Core profit $6.89 a share, +1%; the June quarter alone $1.43, -3%. Next year is mapped at $6.89 to $7.11. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: volumes growing again instead of prices, or a real drawdown with earnings power intact. Verdict: roughly 21 times profit for about 1% growth - nothing wrong with the business, and nothing on offer either.

DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
- Deckers, seventh here and the strongest name across all six boards. This style wants a business priced under what it looks worth, usually after something visible went wrong, and the wrong thing is dated July 23 and counted above. What got marked down with it: $84.50 is $40.38 / 32.3% below the $124.88 this stock reached on September 5 last year, about 11.4 times the middle of Deckers' own map for this year - $7.35 to $7.50 a share, which the company RAISED by five cents in July. Underneath sit $1.603B of cash, no borrowings at all, and a gross margin that went UP while growth halved. A brand genuinely losing its pull does not usually widen its margin. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: HOKA sliding from 7.7% toward zero, at which point 11.4 times is the right price for a brand that stopped compounding, not a discount. Verdict: the discount is real and so is the balance sheet, and the test is the October quarter - expected around October 22, not yet confirmed by Deckers, with analysts modeling $1.79 a share against the $1.82 earned a year earlier. Less, not more.

GROWTH LEN5:
- Trustmark at $46.06, +$0.24 / +0.52% today. The Jackson, Mississippi bank holding company - branches, wealth management and insurance, 2,543 staff. This style wants expansion nobody is overpaying for, and Trustmark pairs the two most cheaply on that board: five straight profitable years, at under 12 times the last year of profit and 1.24 times book value, what the accounts say each share owns. The July 28 quarter: net income $63.5M, $1.08 a share; strip out one-off items and $56.7M, $0.97. Net interest margin - the gap between what it earns on loans and pays on deposits - 3.84%, up 0.03 points on the quarter. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: loan losses rising or that margin rolling over, either of which turns a low multiple into an accurate one. Verdict: cheap and genuinely profitable, and small enough that one region's economy decides it.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
- Reddit at $156.25 (after hours), after finishing the regular day at $155.99, -$2.11 / -1.33%. The San Francisco company runs the discussion forums and sells advertising beside the conversations. This style wants early AND fast, and Reddit is second because every stretch of its record agrees rather than one loud quarter. July 30: revenue $805M, +61%, an eighth straight quarter above 60%; advertising $762M, +64%; daily users 130.3M, +18%; net profit $253M against $89M a year earlier, and no borrowings. The shares fell about 11% on that report anyway, because US user growth was clipped by choppy referral traffic arriving from Google. They sit 44.9% under the $282.95 reached last September 18. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: the deals licensing Reddit's archive to Google and OpenAI renewing on worse terms. Verdict: growth is not the open question here. Who controls the traffic is, and a contract settles that, not a quarter.

INCOME LEN5:
- Lincoln National at $45.87 (after hours), after finishing the regular day at $45.66, +$1.54 / +3.49% - the biggest move of the six today. The Radnor, Pennsylvania company sells life insurance, annuities and workplace benefits as Lincoln Financial. This style watches cash genuinely reaching owners and funded by the business, and what earns Lincoln its place is not the size of the yield but the room behind it. The dividend is $0.45 a quarter, $1.80 a year, near 3.9% of the price - against $2.24 of adjusted operating profit in the June quarter alone, so it takes roughly a fifth of what the business earns. July 30: adjusted operating income $439M, an eighth consecutive quarter of growth. Then the dated part - on August 10 the board declared that same $0.45 and said it plans to restart buying back stock in the third quarter, the one running now. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: the payment finally rising, which is what all that room is for, or operating profit stalling. Verdict: the best-covered payout on the board and the least generous, because the company keeps choosing buybacks over raises.

Five of these six are priced where they are because of something the business did. Deckers is the one where the market did the moving: in twelve months it decided a brand growing 19.8% and a brand growing 7.7% are not the same asset, and marked the whole company down by a third. That judgment is either early or wrong, and October is when the next evidence lands.

Not investment advice.

He frames this as the fundamental miscalculation: believing that America's post-war advantages can be sustained indefinitely .
